lead: A window full of widgets with no positions is a pile of parts on a table. A geometry manager — other toolkits say layout manager — reads what each widget asks for and works out its position and size in pixels inside the container that holds it. Menus turn program actions into words along the top of the window, so the user clicks File and then Exit instead of hunting for buttons. Message boxes stop the program and ask one small question, such as Close?, and hand the answer back as a value. Every desktop form, from an IRCTC booking screen to a college fee portal, is built from these three pieces.
prereq: You need: 6.4 for widgets, the root window and callbacks, and Unit 2 for if statements.

sections.h3: Placing widgets: pack, grid and place

blocks.text: A widget appears only after a geometry manager knows about it. Creating a Label is not enough; the call that places it decides its position and size inside its master, the container that holds it. Tkinter has three managers, and each answers a different question.

pack() stacks widgets in the order they are packed, along one side of the master. side takes 'top' (the default), 'bottom', 'left' or 'right'. fill takes 'x', 'y', 'both' or 'none' and stretches the widget to the master's width, height or both. expand=True gives the spare space to this widget when the window grows; expand=False leaves that space unused. padx and pady add empty pixels outside the widget.

grid() puts widgets into cells of an invisible table. row and column count from 0, so row 0 is the first row. sticky says which sides of its cell a widget sticks to: 'w' left, 'e' right, 'n' top, 's' bottom, and combinations such as 'ew' or 'nsew' to stretch. Without sticky the widget sits centred at its natural size. rowspan and columnspan let one widget cover several cells, and padx, pady add empty pixels around the widget inside its cell; the cell grows to fit widget plus padding.

place() is the third manager: you give x and y in pixels from the top-left of the master, or relx and rely as fractions from 0 to 1. Nothing reflows on resize, so it suits canvas overlays and fixed drawings. The hard rule: one manager per container. Calling pack() on one child and grid() on another child of the same master stops the program with a mixed-manager error. Two frames side by side may each use a different manager.

blocks.text: A menu bar is itself a widget, a Menu attached to the root with root.config(menu=bar). Entries are added by method calls, not fixed at creation, so a menu can change while the program runs.

Two methods do most of the work. add_command(label='Exit', command=close_app) adds a clickable item that calls the function close_app. add_cascade(label='File', menu=file_menu) adds an item that opens another Menu, which is how File, Edit and Help are built. add_separator() draws a thin dividing line. Create menus with tearoff=0; otherwise Tkinter adds a dotted line that lets the user tear the menu off into a floating window.

A Menubutton is a button with a menu hanging under it, used in the window body rather than in the bar. Create the button, create a Menu whose master is that button, link them with mb.config(menu=m), then add commands to m.

A Toplevel is a second top-level window owned by the root: win = Toplevel(root), then set win.title(...) and place widgets inside it. Closing a Toplevel destroys only that window, so the root and the rest of the program keep running. About boxes, settings dialogs and preview windows are Toplevels.

sections.h3: Message boxes and standard widget attributes

blocks.text: A message box is a ready-made dialog that stops the program until the user answers. Import it with from tkinter import messagebox. messagebox.showinfo('Saved', 'File written') shows one line of information with an OK button. messagebox.showwarning(...) adds a caution icon, and messagebox.showerror(...) an error icon. The first argument is the window title, the second the message text.

For questions use askyesno('Exit', 'Close?'): it shows Yes and No buttons and returns the Boolean True for Yes and False for No. askokcancel also returns a Boolean, True for OK. Because the call blocks, the next line runs only after the click; the dialog is modal. These are functions of the messagebox module, not methods of a widget.

Most widgets accept the same standard attributes. relief picks the border look: 'flat', 'raised', 'sunken', 'groove', 'ridge' or 'solid'. borderwidth (short form bd) gives border thickness in pixels, and a relief stays invisible while borderwidth is 0. width and height set size in characters for text widgets and in pixels for frames. fg and bg set text and background colour, font the typeface, state ('normal' or 'disabled') whether the user can act on it, and cursor the pointer shape. Pass these when creating the widget, or later through config().

figure.caption: The File menu's Exit item calls askyesno; only a Yes answer reaches destroy(), which closes the root window.

spec.title: menu to dialog
spec.aria: A window menu bar leads to a File menu, an Exit item, an askyesno dialog with the question Close?, and then destroy().

examples.question: A Tkinter window has a File menu whose Exit item asks messagebox.askyesno('Exit', 'Close?') and calls root.destroy() only when the reply is true. Below the menu a Frame holds a Label at row 0, column 0 and an Entry at row 0, column 1, both created with padx=6. (a) Write the code for the menu, the Exit callback and the two grid calls. (b) What exactly does askyesno return? (c) What is the first grid row number? (d) How many pixels of horizontal padding does row 0 add?
steps: Create the bar: bar = Menu(root), then root.config(menu=bar). One Menu widget holds the whole bar.
Create the submenu: file_menu = Menu(bar, tearoff=0) and link it with bar.add_cascade(label='File', menu=file_menu).
Add the item: file_menu.add_command(label='Exit', command=close_app). The callback holds the question, not the menu.
Write the callback: def close_app(): answer = messagebox.askyesno('Exit', 'Close?'); if answer: root.destroy(). answer is True for Yes and False for No, so if answer: runs destroy only on Yes.
Place the two widgets: label.grid(row=0, column=0, padx=6) and entry.grid(row=0, column=1, padx=6). Grid numbering starts at 0, so the first row is 0.
Count padding: each widget with padx=6 adds 6 px on each of its two sides, which is 12 px per widget. Row 0 holds 2 widgets, so the row carries 2 × 12 = 24 px of horizontal padding.
Return value: askyesno gives a Boolean, True (1) for Yes and False (0) for No. It never gives the string 'yes'.
examples.answer: askyesno returns the Boolean True (1) or False (0); the first grid row is 0; row 0 carries 2 widgets × 2 sides × 6 px = 24 px of horizontal padding.
examples.check:
widgets = 2
sides = 2
padx = 6
print(widgets * sides * padx)
print(0)

traps: Never call pack() and grid() on children of the same master; the program stops with a mixed-manager error. Put the second group inside its own Frame.
askyesno returns a Boolean, not the string 'yes'. The test if answer == 'yes': is always false; write if answer:.
grid counts from 0, so the first row and first column are 0, not 1. A widget put at row 1 leaves row 0 empty unless something fills it.
fill and expand do different jobs: fill='both' stretches a widget into the space it already has, and only expand=True wins it the extra space when the window grows.
relief='raised' shows only a 1-pixel bevel with the default borderwidth; set borderwidth=2 or more to see it clearly. With borderwidth=0 no relief is visible at all.

quiz.q: Name the three Tkinter geometry managers and the value each uses to position a widget.
quiz.a: pack uses side and packing order; grid uses row and column; place uses x and y, or relx and rely as fractions.

quiz.q: Why does Tkinter refuse to mix pack and grid in one container, and how do you place two differently managed groups in one window?
quiz.a: Each container has a single layout engine; two managers would compute positions for the same children and clash, so Tkinter stops with an error. Wrap each group in its own Frame, and let one frame use pack and the other grid.

quiz.q: A Frame holds a Label at row 0 column 0 and an Entry at row 0 column 1, both with padx=4 and pady=2. Write the two grid calls and compute the total horizontal and total vertical padding added in that row.
quiz.a: label.grid(row=0, column=0, padx=4, pady=2) and entry.grid(row=0, column=1, padx=4, pady=2). Horizontal: the two widgets sit in different columns, so 2 widgets × 2 sides × 4 px = 16 px. Vertical: both widgets share row 0, so the row height is the taller widget plus 2 px at the top and 2 px at the bottom, that is 4 px of added vertical padding; the pady of the two widgets does not double.

quiz.q: A student writes answer = messagebox.askyesno('Exit','Close?') and then if answer == 'Yes': root.destroy(). The user clicks Yes and the window never closes. Explain what went wrong and fix it.
quiz.a: askyesno returns the Boolean True, and True == 'Yes' is False, so destroy() is never reached. Fix it with if answer: or if answer == True:. Printing answer shows True, never the word Yes.

quiz.q: What is the difference between add_command and add_cascade on a Menu, and what does tearoff=0 do?
quiz.a: add_command adds a clickable item that runs a callback; add_cascade adds an item that opens another Menu as a submenu. tearoff=0 removes the dashed tear-off entry so the menu cannot be detached into its own window.

quiz.q: A toolbar Frame is packed at the top with fill='x', then a body Frame with fill='both', expand=True. The user maximises the window. Say which frame grows, and what changes if expand=True is removed from the body frame.
quiz.a: The toolbar stretches only horizontally and keeps its height. The body frame takes all remaining width and height, because fill='both' with expand=True claims the spare space. Without expand=True the body keeps its natural size and the extra space stays empty at the bottom of the window.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real toolkits split the same job differently: Qt uses layout classes such as QVBoxLayout, and GTK uses boxes and grids with expand flags. Web layout borrows the idea directly — CSS grid and flexbox are geometry managers in all but name. Declarative toolkits such as Flutter, SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose let you describe the widget tree and let the runtime place it. Accessibility work starts here too, because a layout with no sensible reading order confuses screen readers. Search next: 'tkinter ttk widgets', 'Qt Designer layouts', 'CSS grid versus flexbox'.
